title: List, Dict, and Set Comprehensions
description: Transform and filter data concisely with list, set, and dict comprehensions, nested readability boundaries, and generator expressions.
learning_objectives: Construct expressive list comprehensions combining transformation and filtering
Build deduplicated set comprehensions and key-value mapping dict comprehensions
Maintain nested readability boundaries without writing unmaintainable one-liners
Differentiate memory usage between materialized comprehensions and generator expressions

sections.title: List comprehension syntax and mechanics
sections.learning_objective: Write clean list comprehensions to transform sequences.
sections.markdown: A list comprehension provides a concise syntax for creating a new list by transforming items from an iterable. The standard structure is `[expression for item in iterable]`. Under the hood, Python optimizes comprehensions into specialized bytecode that avoids repeated `.append()` attribute lookups, making them noticeably faster than equivalent manual accumulator loops. Keep expressions focused on a single transformation; if the transformation requires multiple side effects or statements, use an explicit for loop.

examples.code:
raw_prices = [19.99, 5.50, 40.0, 120.0]
with_tax = [round(price * 1.08, 2) for price in raw_prices]
print(with_tax)
examples.explanation: Each price is multiplied by 1.08 and rounded, materializing a new list in a single expression.

key_points: List comprehensions map an expression across an iterable to produce a new list.
Comprehensions are faster than manual append loops due to specialized C-level bytecode.
sections.checkpoint: Contrast [x * 2 for x in data] with a traditional accumulator loop in terms of readability and performance.

sections.title: Filtering with conditions vs conditional expressions
sections.learning_objective: Apply filtering conditions and ternary branching correctly within comprehensions.
sections.markdown: Conditions in comprehensions serve two distinct purposes based on placement. A trailing `if condition` at the end filters elements: only items satisfying the condition are included. Conversely, a ternary conditional expression `value_if_true if condition else value_if_false` placed at the beginning transforms every item, altering the output value while preserving the element count. Mixing up their placement is a common beginner error.

examples.code:
scores = [85, 42, 91, 58, 77]
passing = [s for s in scores if s >= 60]
labels = ['pass' if s >= 60 else 'fail' for s in scores]
print(f'Filtered: {passing}')
print(f'Transformed: {labels}')
examples.explanation: Trailing if filters items (<60 excluded); ternary if-else at the start maps every score to a label.

key_points: Trailing if condition filters out non-matching elements.
Leading ternary expr if cond else expr maps every element to an alternate value.
sections.checkpoint: Why does [x for x in data if x % 2 == 0 else 0] cause a SyntaxError in Python?

sections.title: Dict comprehensions and set comprehensions
sections.learning_objective: Build mappings and unique sets with comprehension syntax.
sections.markdown: Python extends comprehensions to sets and dictionaries. A set comprehension uses curly braces `{expr for item in iterable}` to construct a unique, deduplicated collection in O(n) time. A dict comprehension uses key-value syntax `{key_expr: value_expr for item in iterable}`. Common applications include inverting key-value pairs in a dictionary, filtering out invalid configuration entries, or mapping object IDs directly to object instances for constant-time lookups.

examples.explanation: Set comprehension eliminates duplicate roles; dict comprehension indexes roles by integer user ID.

key_points: Set comprehensions {x for x in s} automatically deduplicate values.
Dict comprehensions {k: v for ...} build lookup tables and index datasets.
sections.checkpoint: Write a dict comprehension that inverts a dictionary mapping unique usernames to user IDs.

sections.title: Nested comprehensions and nested readability boundaries
sections.learning_objective: Flatten matrices and identify when nesting harms code maintainability.
sections.markdown: Comprehensions can contain multiple `for` clauses, matching the order of nested loops. For example, flattening a 2D matrix uses `[cell for row in matrix for cell in row]`: the outer loop comes first, followed by the inner loop. However, engineers must respect nested readability boundaries: when a comprehension requires multiple loops, complex nested conditions, or exceeds two lines, replace it with an explicit multi-line loop. Comprehensions should simplify comprehension, not obscure business logic.

examples.code:
matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
flattened_evens = [x for row in matrix for x in row if x % 2 == 0]
print(f'Flattened evens: {flattened_evens}')
examples.explanation: Iterates each row, then each element x in that row, keeping only even integers.

key_points: Clause order in nested comprehensions follows the order of standard nested for loops.
Respect nested readability: avoid triple loops or dense logic in a single expression.
sections.checkpoint: Rewrite a 2-level nested comprehension as a standard nested for-loop with append.

sections.title: Generator expressions vs list comprehensions
sections.learning_objective: Select between eager list materialization and lazy generator streaming.
sections.markdown: A generator expression uses parentheses instead of brackets: `(expr for item in iterable)`. While list comprehensions eagerly allocate and populate the entire list in memory, generator expressions evaluate lazily, producing items one at a time on demand. When passing data into consumer functions like `sum()`, `max()`, `min()`, or `any()`, a generator expression avoids allocating auxiliary O(n) memory, making it ideal for processing massive log files or database result streams.

examples.code:
import sys
list_comp = [x * x for x in range(1000)]
gen_exp = (x * x for x in range(1000))
print(f'List size bytes: {sys.getsizeof(list_comp)}')
print(f'Gen size bytes: {sys.getsizeof(gen_exp)}')
print('Total sum:', sum(x * x for x in range(5)))
examples.explanation: The generator expression maintains an O(1) constant memory footprint regardless of item count.
examples.expected_output:
List size bytes: 8856
Gen size bytes: 200
Total sum: 30

key_points: List comprehensions materialize all items immediately in O(n) memory.
Generator expressions stream items on demand with O(1) memory.
sections.checkpoint: When should you choose a list comprehension over a generator expression?

sections.title: Interview check and practice
sections.learning_objective: Answer interview questions on comprehensions and practice in Coding Arena.
sections.markdown:
Comprehensions are frequent topics in technical screens to evaluate clean code habits.

### Oral Interview Questions
1. *What is the scope of loop variables in a Python 3 list comprehension compared to a standard for loop?*
   *(In Python 3, comprehensions have their own local function-like scope, preventing loop variable leakage into outer scope).*
2. *How do memory footprints differ between `[x for x in stream]` and `(x for x in stream)`?*
3. *When does a comprehension become an anti-pattern?*

### Code Trace Challenge
Trace this dict comprehension: `words = ['apple', 'bat', 'car', 'apple']; d = {w: len(w) for w in words}`. The duplicate 'apple' key simply overwrites itself, resulting in `{'apple': 5, 'bat': 3, 'car': 3}`.

### Common Interview Trap
Using a list comprehension purely for its side effects without using the returned list (e.g. `[print(x) for x in items]`). This needlessly allocates an array of `[None, None, ...]` in memory. Use a standard `for` loop whenever side effects are the primary objective.

### Arena Practice Problems
Test your comprehension fluency in Coding Arena:
- `python-deduplicate-list`: Sequence filtering and preserving order
- `python-word-count`: Frequency mapping and dictionary accumulation
- `python-running-sum`: Transforming numerical arrays

examples.code:
names = ['alice', 'bob', 'charlie']
uppers = [n.upper() for n in names if len(n) > 3]
print(uppers)
examples.explanation: Filters names with length > 3 and maps them to uppercase.

key_points: Do not use comprehensions for side effects; use standard loops.
Comprehensions in Python 3 do not leak loop variables into outer scopes.
sections.checkpoint: Demonstrate why [print(x) for x in range(3)] is an anti-pattern.

summary: List comprehensions provide concise, performant sequence transformation and filtering.
Set and dict comprehensions cleanly construct unique sets and indexed mappings.
Condition placement dictates whether elements are filtered (trailing if) or transformed (ternary).
Nested comprehensions follow loop ordering but must respect readability boundaries.
Generator expressions evaluate lazily, consuming O(1) memory for streaming operations.
interview_takeaways: Avoid using comprehensions solely for side effects like printing or logging.
Prefer generator expressions when passing data directly into aggregators like sum() or any().
Refactor multi-line or nested comprehensions into explicit loops to maintain readability.
common_mistakes: Placing an else clause after a trailing if filter instead of using leading ternary syntax
Writing unreadable 3-level nested comprehensions instead of clean helper functions
Using list comprehensions for massive streams where generator expressions prevent OOM crashes
Using a comprehension when an in-place mutation or standard loop is clearer
